standard_prerequisites.name: Behaviour of the inverse image of the subscheme under a point blowup
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Same chapter, the lemma describing the blowup of a regular surface at a closed point and the description of the strict transform of a curve under such a blowup
standard_prerequisites.use: Supplies the facts that the exceptional divisor is a regular curve and that the strict transform of a component is either the component itself or its blowup at the point, so no new singular one dimensional components appear.

standard_prerequisites.name: Making the subscheme an effective Cartier divisor with regular components
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Same chapter, the lemnas turning the subscheme of the surface into an effective Cartier divisor and making its components regular by blowups in closed points
standard_prerequisites.use: Supplies the reduction to the case where the subscheme is an effective Cartier divisor with regular irreducible components.

standard_prerequisites.name: Multiplicity invariant of the intersection of two regular curves and its behaviour under blowup
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Same chapter, the definition of the multiplicity of the intersection of two curves and the lemma computing its behaviour under a blowup of the intersection points
standard_prerequisites.use: Supplies the invariant used for the descending induction, together with the fact that the new invariants against the exceptional divisor are one.

standard_prerequisites.name: Criterion for a divisor with regular components to be strict normal crossings
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Etale Morphisms, the lemma characterizing a strict normal crossings divisor through the local shape of the components at every point
standard_prerequisites.use: Supplies the final recognition of the divisor as a strict normal crossings divisor.

core_obligations: Reduce to a Cartier divisor with regular components (proof lines 4461-4476): blowing up a closed point of the surface replaces the subscheme by the union of its strict transform and the exceptional divisor; the exceptional divisor is regular and the strict transforms of the components of dimension one are either unchanged or blowups of the components at the point, so no new singular curves are produced; the cited lemmas then allow one to assume that the subscheme is an effective Cartier divisor all of whose irreducible components are regular.

Decrease the maximal multiplicity (proof lines 4478-4492): having regular components, consider the invariant given by the multiplicity of the intersection of two components at a common point and blow up all points where the maximum is attained; the behaviour of the invariant under blowup shows that the maximum strictly decreases, while the new invariants against the exceptional divisor are equal to one.

Separate the components (proof lines 4492-4498): once the maximum equals one, blow up the points where more than two components meet; afterwards the components meeting at a point are at most two and their intersection multiplicity is one, which by the local criterion means precisely that the divisor is a strict normal crossings divisor.
proof_roadmap: Use point blowups to turn the subscheme into an effective Cartier divisor with regular components, checking that no new singular curves appear.
Run a descending induction on the maximal intersection multiplicity of two components.
Blow up the points where more than two components meet to reach the strict normal crossings situation.
difficulty_reason: The lemma proves that for a proper closed subscheme of a regular surface whose one dimensional components satisfy the equivalent conditions of the curve resolution lemma, a sequence of blowups in closed points makes the inverse image an effective Cartier divisor supported on a strict normal crossings divisor (statement lines 4447-4459). The proof (proof lines 4461-4501) reduces to a Cartier divisor with regular components, decreases the maximal intersection multiplicity of two components by blowing up the relevant points, and separates the components meeting in more than two branches. H3: a reduction with a descending induction on an explicit invariant, written out in full.
